haiku-low.q1: They see the generic message: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
haiku-low.q2: Once 3 or more rows exist in the last hour, they get the generic message and stop. No link is sent and no row is created.
haiku-low.q3: A link works for 30 minutes after creation. It ends sooner when used to set a password or when a newer link revokes it.
haiku-low.q4: The link stays usable. The form is shown again, and the row is not marked used or revoked.
haiku-low.q5: No devices stay logged in, because all the user's sessions are deleted. The user is redirected to login and must sign in again.
haiku-low.q6: The worker retries 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. The user is not told and gets no email.
haiku-low.q7: The raw token is put in the reset email job when the link is requested. The worker sends that job, so the token reaches the user. Only its hash is stored.
haiku-low.q8: It hashes the token from the link and finds the matching row. The link is good only if the row is not expired, used or revoked. Nothing is changed.
haiku-low.q9: It is counted from the reset_tokens rows created in the last hour. Older rows drop out of that window as time passes.
haiku-low.q10: Within the same transaction that inserts the new row, the older unused rows are revoked. This happens before the reset email is queued.
haiku-low.q11: The password hash update, marking the row used, and deleting sessions happen together in one transaction. The confirmation email is queued afterward, and only if that step succeeds.

sonnet.q1: They see the generic message: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is sent.
sonnet.q2: The count of reset_tokens rows in the last hour (including revoked and used) is already 3 or more, so the user sees the generic message and no link is sent.
sonnet.q3: 30 minutes from creation (expires_at = created_at + 30 minutes). It can end sooner if it is used (successful reset) or revoked by a newer link.
sonnet.q4: Still valid and usable: the form is shown again and the link is not used up.
sonnet.q5: None. All sessions are deleted, so the user is logged out everywhere. They are redirected to the login page (not logged in automatically) and log in with the new password.
sonnet.q6: The worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. Nobody is told, so the user gets no email and must ask again.
sonnet.q7: The raw token is generated in step 1 and put in the link inside the queued reset email job. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored in the table.
sonnet.q8: It hashes the token from the link and finds the row with that hash. The row is good if it exists and is not expired, not used and not revoked.
sonnet.q9: NOT STATED as a separate counter. The count is taken from reset_tokens rows created in the last hour (includes revoked and used rows). Old requests drop out as their created_at passes one hour old; the exact query mechanism is not stated.
sonnet.q10: In step 1, in the same transaction that inserts the new row, the user's older unused rows are revoked.
sonnet.q11: In one transaction: store the new password hash, mark the reset row used, and delete all the user's sessions. The "password changed" email is queued after that transaction commits.
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED. The document only says the transaction marks the row used; it does not describe handling of simultaneous submissions.
